newsitem.title: USA: Governors to fight Medicaid cuts in budget proposal.
newsitem.headline: Governors to fight Medicaid cuts in budget proposal.

text.p: The nation's governors vowed Thursday to fight an emerging balanced budget deal that would cap federal spending on the Medicaid health programme for the poor, elderly and disabled.

The White House and Republicans are close to an agreement cutting about $25 billion from Medicaid over five years. The plan puts an annual ceiling on federal aid and scales back payments to hospitals that serve a large number of the poor.
The governors warned the cap would result in a huge cost shift to the states, forcing them to cut poor women and children off the programme if caseload growth was higher than expected.

"Governors are concerned a budget agreement ... may fundamentally break the long-standing partnership between the states and the federal government to provide health care to the most vulnerable of our citizens," Nevada Democratic Gov. Bob Miller and Ohio Republican Gov. George Voinovich said in a statement.
The two made their comments on behalf of the National Governors' Association.
The White House and Republicans are close to final agreement on an overall plan to balance the budget over five years.
Medicaid, which provides health care for 37 million poor, elderly and disabled Americans is an open-ended entitlement. That means anyone who meets eligibility criteria automatically receives aid.
The programme, jointly funded by states and the federal government, also pays more than half the nation's nursing home bills.
Governors worry that if federal aid is limited, they will have to pay more of the costs for the programme should caseloads increase faster than expected.
The White House believes a cap is needed to control future spending on the programme, which had been growing at double-digit rates in the 1980s. Programme costs rose only about 3.3 percent last year.
The cap would account for only part of the Medicaid savings; more than half would come from limiting hospital aid.

"What they're doing to Medicaid is absolutely outrageous ... it's going to be arbitrary and chaotic," said California Democratic Representative Henry Waxman, a long-time champion of the Medicaid programme.
The strong, bipartisan opposition of the National Governors' Association is likely to make it harder for the White House to sell any budget deal that includes a cap.
